_: The dotted-name contract, as cases. `src/dunneflow/ingest/dotted.py` is the contract
itself; this is what proves a reader keeps it. Every `exact`, `prefix`, `method` and
`contains` in every detectors YAML is matched against this spelling, so a reader that
spells it differently makes every rule miss — and a map with no boundaries, no ways in
and no CLI looks exactly like a program that has none.
`expect` is a dotted form the reader must record for the snippet. `expect: ""` means
the reader must record **no call at all** — rule 3, where the chain cannot be named.
A case with no snippet for a language is a rule that language has no syntax for; the
runner names it unexercised and never counts it as passing.

cases.why: a chain of one is still a chain
a call in the middle folds to its callee — reading a file this way is one of the commonest boundary touches there is
no name at the root, so nothing may be matched against a rule
a subscript anywhere kills the chain: naming it would mean deciding what handlers['x'] is, and deciding that is resolution
the written library prefix, never the resolved one — rules are written against the spelling people use
`from json import loads` then `loads(x)` is `loads`, not `json.loads`
a type argument is not part of the name
`new Foo()` is `Foo` **and** carries `is_construction`, so the two spellings stay two facts — asserting only the name would pass on a reader that had flattened them (rule 37)
the receiver word as written; each language declares its own in receiver_words
Python declares two receiver words and both are written as written
TypeScript's receiver word is `this`, written as written and never expanded
